1afe48964a94a6d8: The compose-bridge FeatureRecipe is the canonical boundary-scope-FR pattern. A `core/compose-bridge` feature is attached at a parent boundary that contains two sub-boundaries (e.g., `services-net` and `data-net`) with shared `directory:`. Its `executionScope: boundary` runs the FR once per parent-boundary attachment. The FR forwards the boundary's `internal_uses_edges` to the compose provider, which selects the edges whose endpoints land on different networks, derives a gateway listen port per edge (the target's own port, with a `portBase` collision fallback), generates one nginx `stream` `server` block per bridged edge (`listen <port>; set $uN <target-host>:<target-port>; proxy_pass $uN;`, under a `resolver` directive so each upstream resolves at connection time rather than once at startup; the `$` in those variables is escaped to `$$` so Docker Compose's `$`-interpolation leaves a literal `$` for nginx), and delivers the aggregated config as a mounted compose config — a top-level `configs:` entry with inline `content:`, referenced from `aggrega-gw` and mounted at `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` (so nginx loads it without an authored `command:`). Inline `configs.content` requires Docker Compose ≥ 2.23.1. From the **same** per-edge derivation, the boundary→component env channel rewrites each consumer's host env var (e.g. `DB_HOST`) to `aggrega-gw:<port>` — so the gateway's `listen` and the consumer's rewrite agree per edge by construction, including the `portBase`-reassigned collisions. The rewrite applies to a key the consumer's own connection delivered, which is interception; where another Feature attached to the consumer delivered that key — through its `inject:` block, its `injectMapping`, or a boundary Feature's override of its own — the build halts naming both Features rather than replace that delivery (see "A Feature attached to a boundary overrides a key another attached Feature delivered" in [fatal-halts.md](../errors/fatal-halts.md)). The gateway also joins **every network its bridged edges span** (the consumer's network and the target's), so at runtime the consumer can reach `aggrega-gw:<port>` and the gateway can `proxy_pass` to the target — the relay path resolves end-to-end. The per-(path, provider) compose assembler merges the gateway alongside the per-component contributors at the same evaluated path: one `docker-compose.yaml` containing every component plus the bridge gateway. The upstream is a deterministic compile-time compose service pointer; compose's runtime DNS resolves it (no compile-time runtime resolution).

27b931354176f764: **A client can also stop one call without stopping the server, and how it does so is the transport's.** Calls are answered concurrently, so ending one is acted on while that call is still running rather than waiting behind it. Over standard input and output a client names the call's id; cancelling a call that has already been answered, or one the server is not working on, does nothing — which is what makes such a message safe to send without first knowing whether the answer is already on its way back. Over HTTP there is no message to send: closing the connection that carried the call ends it. 3442c41536cf755e: **Prompt-injection screening:** `core/prompt-injection-shield` declares that the model requests a gateway forwards are checked, before the model is called, for an attempt to override the instructions the model was given, at a `sensitivity` of `standard` or `strict` — strict refusing more such attempts, and more legitimate requests with them. The check is a probabilistic classifier's verdict: it misses some attacks — reworded, encoded or respelled ones among them — refuses some legitimate requests, and is known to be evadable, so it is one control beside others, and it does not judge the model's reply, tool-call arguments or images. It attaches to any gateway, and a realization either sends the gateway's requests through a guard wired to its `guard` socket, which needs nothing of the gateway but that it forwards to an address it is configured with, or turns on a check the gateway runs itself. Through a guard, the guard checks each request and forwards what it admits to the model, and attaching the Feature with nothing on that socket halts the build naming it. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway and on the NGINX gateway, each with `core/security/nemo-guardrails` as the guard: a service speaking the OpenAI chat-completions API, whose rail sends the latest user message of a request to the classifier of the `core/security/trustyai-huggingface-detector` wired to it and refuses the request when that classifier's score reaches the guard's threshold. A refused request is answered by the guard itself, with an ordinary completion, and nothing of it reaches the model; when the guard or its detector cannot be reached the request is refused too. Each of the two halts the build unless the guard is that one, running the threshold the sensitivity names — 0.5 for `standard` and 0.001 for `strict`, the two values measured for the detector's default classifier, which the gateway, seeing the guard and not the detector behind it, cannot check the model of. On the AI gateway every alias of the model map is sent to the guard, each target written `openai/<model>`, so the map is the one typed by hand: a model wired to the gateway's `models` socket would be sent to its own endpoint with its own connection's credential, past the guard, and the realization halts the build while that socket holds a connection, naming it. The AI gateway refuses every request but a chat completion, the one kind the guard checks; on the NGINX gateway its one location forwards to the guard in place of the upstream, and the guard answers no other model route. On `core/gateway/azure-api-management` it is realized as Azure's own prompt shield, turned on in the API's policy through the instance's Azure AI Content Safety backend that `infra.content_safety_backend_id` names, and the build halts while that key is unset: Azure AI Content Safety checks each request for a user attack before the model is called, ahead of a semantic cache's lookup, and the gateway answers one it detects with HTTP 403, as it answers a request longer than the service accepts. The shield is on or off, so `standard` is kept and `strict` is refused by name, and it runs at Microsoft's own sensitivity, not measured against the threshold `standard` names on the guards. The instance reaches that backend with its managed identity, which needs the Cognitive Services User role on the service; the build sees neither. No gateway in the standard library but these three realizes it, and attaching it to another halts the build naming the type: most render no route a realization could send through a guard — they keep their routes in a store of their own, take them from the services behind them, or are a hosted service on which the standard library turns on no check of this kind — and `core/gateway/apisix`, whose chart Recipe renders the routes of the models wired to it, and `core/gateway/envoy-gateway`, whose Recipe renders the AI route of the models wired to it, have no realization of it. On `core/gateway/agentgateway`, whose Recipes render an entry for each model wired to it, the realization halts every attachment, naming why: agentgateway judges a request for such an attempt only through a service it calls — a webhook the operator runs, or Azure AI Content Safety, Google Model Armor or AWS Bedrock Guardrails — and the realization wires none of them. On `core/gateway/higress` the realization halts every attachment too, naming why: Higress judges such an attempt only through a service it calls — Alibaba Cloud's content-security service, or, through a plugin its source carries but its 2.2.5 plugin release does not publish, a Qwen3Guard model service the operator runs — each letting the request through when that call fails, and the realization wires neither. On `core/gateway/traefik-hub` the realization halts every attachment as well, naming why: Traefik Hub judges such an attempt only through a service it calls — its LLM Guard and Parallel LLM Guard middlewares, which call a guard service or a model in a request and with conditions the realization would have to write, and whose work with a prompt-attack detector is not measured, so no sensitivity maps to a check there; or its Azure Prompt Shield, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and GCP Model Armor middlewares, which call hosted services the realization does not wire. The guard reads only the latest user message, so a system message, an earlier turn or a tool result reaches the model unread, and only traffic crossing the gateway is screened: a workload calling the model's address directly goes around it.

4d0505b0beef2682: **Upstream certificate pinning is the worked case.** A pin is a control over which key an upstream may present: accept only a certificate whose public key matches one the Release supplies. That is a different assertion from requiring an upstream's certificate to chain to a trust anchor the Release supplies, and different again from asserting what a certificate's subject says — both of those state what a certificate must *say*, while a pin states which key it must *be*. Pinning is a separate capability, and at least two independent products implement it for the connections they open to an upstream: Tyk takes the upstream's public key in PEM form, and Envoy takes a hash of it. So it is a Feature, `core/upstream-key-pinning`, whose selector names `dataplane.aggrega.ai/upstream-pinning: public-key`, and what this catalog realizes is answered product by product: `core/gateway/tyk` carries the value and a FeatureRecipe for each of its targets, while the gateways here that embed Envoy expose its pin setting only for the certificates clients present, or not at all, so they carry no value and an attachment to them halts at the selector. A pin narrows what an upstream may present; it is a control, not an assurance that the connection is otherwise sound.
4d18695468204ca1:
**The Deterministic Output Rule (GitOps Safety):**
Because GitOps controllers (ArgoCD, Flux) perform byte-level diff detection on rendered artifacts, the compiler guarantees that identical inputs produce byte-identical outputs. Maps that flow through the template context (`.context.inject.env`, `.values`, `.infra`, and the rest of the runtime view) are backed by ordered-map structures that preserve author insertion order across the data layer; `{{ range }}` over those maps iterates in author order, not in alphabetical order. Ops engineers can rely on iteration order being deterministic across runs of the same input. The Sprig `keys` function, however, returns Go-map iteration order (which is non-deterministic by language design); templates that compose a deterministic key sequence from `keys` output must pipe through `sortAlpha` (e.g., `{{ keys .values | sortAlpha }}`) to recover determinism.

`aggrega registry add --key <file>` copies the file's contents there, and so does pinning a
policy the registry advertises with a key in it. The value is a PEM public-key block — the

matching `-----END` line — and any text above the block is ignored.

6d39770ec3f2cb1c: **The host runtime: a capability-denying sandbox.** Aggrega embeds the Wasm host as the Extism toolkit running on top of the Wazero engine; the host binary stays pure Go with no native toolchain dependency, so `aggrega` cross-compiles cleanly. Every socket runs behind an **AOT-purity firewall**: the host refuses to grant a plugin any runtime-access capability — no network, no filesystem, no wall-clock, no environment, no standard I/O — and rejects a plugin that asks for one. A plugin that cannot reach the network or read the clock cannot break the compiler's ahead-of-time guarantee that the same input produces the same output. Language runtimes that need a few benign startup imports run against a capability-denied configuration of those imports: the host fixes the observable wall clock, supplies real entropy, discards standard I/O, and grants no filesystem, argument, or environment access — so a plugin can reach no host capability that varies across builds. Entropy is deliberately left real rather than pinned: pinning it would stabilise a guest language runtime's internal hash seed and map-iteration order, and so hide a plugin whose own output is not reproducible instead of letting that surface as differing output. A plugin whose result depends on entropy is an authoring-level determinism problem, and this configuration is built to reveal it rather than mask it.

**Stating a rule once: governance attachments are workspace-scoped.**
The two patterns above are authored per component and per Feature, but the governance attachment that enforces them is not. A governance plugin is attached at the workspace configuration's `plugins.governance` key, and that attachment binds **every build in the workspace**. A corporate rule is therefore stated in exactly one place: the platform team attaches the plugin once, and no component, Aggregate or Release has to opt in, mention it, or be edited for it to apply. This is what makes the validation failsafe in pattern 1 a complete answer rather than a per-project convention — a developer who bypasses the internal catalog and requests a naked `core/postgres` is evaluated by the same attached policy as everyone else, because the policy is a property of the workspace rather than of the component they chose.
7000483027a021f9: **Why every catalog YAML repeats the envelope.** The envelope (`apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata` block) appears at the top of every catalog file — Component, Feature, Recipe, FeatureRecipe, Aggregate, Manifest, Release, Plugin — regardless of how short the body is. The repetition is deliberate: each file is designed to parse, validate, lint, and inspect as a standalone artefact. A single file pulled from the OCI registry, dropped into a CI sandbox, or opened in a third-party editor must carry enough self-description that downstream tooling can identify what kind of entity it represents and which schema version applies. Catalog-relative-path inference (where the directory location implies the entity kind and the envelope could be omitted) is not implemented today — every parser, validator, and linter consumes the envelope explicitly. The cost is mechanical boilerplate per file; the benefit is that the standalone-tooling guarantee holds across the OCI distribution surface, the local filesystem, and the IDE / CI / inspect surfaces. Authors copy the envelope from existing files when authoring new catalog content; future scaffolders are expected to ship the boilerplate as starter templates.

7d33a7f08d62f9e6: **Connection credential matches target key** (`connection-credential-matches-target-key`) — a server that checks a key holds the key it verifies in a slot of its own Component, and a caller presents a key on the connection it reaches the server through. Neither end sees the other's attachments, so the two hold one key only because their authors write it at both ends — usually by having both attachments read one parameter — and a build never compares them. This rule does, and it is the one rule that reads a whole Release, so it runs under `--release` and at no other scope. It finds both ends by the names the standard catalog gives them: the target's key is the slot `api_key` its Component declares in `spec.featuresSchema`, and the caller's is the slot `credential` on the connection, written at `uses.<socket>.<alias>.features.credential` in the Aggregate or on a connection the Release wires. For each connection whose target declares `api_key` and is not labelled managed, it reports a connection carrying a credential to a target whose key slot is unfilled, a filled key slot with no credential on the connection, and two ends naming their secret differently. What it compares is each end's locator — the `origin` an attachment writes, in `values` in the Aggregate or `infra` in the Release — as the author wrote it, so two ends reading one parameter compare equal and two literals compare by their text; nothing is resolved, and a finding names the component, the connection, the target and the two slots but **never quotes either locator**, since the text written there can be the secret itself. A target declaring no `api_key` slot draws nothing, and a slot that is not the caller key, such as a model server's registry pull token, is never read. Nor is a target whose Component is labelled `component.aggrega.ai/hosting: managed` judged, whatever its `api_key` slot holds: such a Component stands for a service its vendor runs, so nothing the Release runs checks a key on it, and where it declares `api_key` — the key to a hosted model API, say, under the name the vendor's product gives it — the slot holds the key the Release presents to that vendor, never one its callers present. A target labelled `self-hosted`, `external` or `mixed`, or carrying no hosting label, is judged. A connection on the socket `scrape_target` — the name the standard catalog gives the socket a metrics scraper reaches its targets through — is a scrape, and whether a scrape's credential should be the target's caller key depends on the target's product: some serve their metrics with no credential, some put them behind the key every caller presents, and some take a token of their own. So for a scrape the rule reads what the target's Component states in its annotation `observability.aggrega.ai/metrics-credential`: under `none` the scrape is not judged at all; under `separate-token` its credential is never compared with the target's `api_key`, so none of the three findings is reported on it; under `target-key` it is judged like any other connection. The rule reads only those three values, so a scrape to a target without the annotation, or with any other value, is judged like any other connection — and every connection on another socket, a model, tool or datastore connection included, is judged the same whatever the target's annotation says. It reads the attachments written on the target and on the connection: an `api_key` attachment reaching the target from a subsystem or a boundary instead leaves that connection unjudged, one an annotation adds is not among them, so a key slot filled only that way reads as unfilled, an end whose attachment writes no locator is compared only for whether it is filled, and a component an imported module contributes is not read. Because the slot names, the hosting label, the scrape socket's name and the metrics annotation are catalog conventions no schema keyword marks, a catalog naming the slots differently draws nothing, a scraping socket named differently is judged like any other socket, and a Component that holds a vendor's key in a slot named `api_key` without the managed label is read as a target checking that key, since the slot's name, the label and the annotation are all the rule reads of a target's Component. Default on; opt out with `allow_connection_credential_mismatches`.

**Centralized Enterprise Governance (Evaluating Complete Reality):**
Relying on out-of-band mechanisms (like `CODEOWNERS` on a git repository) to govern architecture is a weak workaround. All governance is localized in the compiler's governance verdict roles. Because the AOT compiler builds the IR Graph by flattening *both* the Developer's `Aggregate` and the Ops Engineer's `Release`, the policy engine evaluates the complete reality before physical artifacts are generated. Policies can fatally halt the build if a developer requests an unapproved Component, if Ops maps a component to an unapproved Recipe in the Manifest, or if an insecure Wasm mutation is attached to a Component carrying a `restricted` subsystem label.
91d5cc1ce607e467: **An alignment reports whether it changed anything, and that is the field to act on.** `changed` separates a write from an alignment that found the records already correct: an unchanged file was left byte-identical, so a client holding that document has nothing to reload, and running the request twice reports no change the second time. `entity` names the file, `hostFunctions` carries the derived set, and `commands` carries the mirror as values rather than as the line a terminal prints — each entry a `name`, an optional `description`, and `flags`, each flag carrying its `name` and its optional `shorthand`, `description`, `type` and `default`. The write is atomic, so a client reading that file while the alignment runs never observes a partial document.
91d608780ef9bf3f: Because the Aggrega compiler is mathematically unopinionated, it possesses zero hardcoded knowledge of AI frameworks, token budgets, or memory partitioning. Instead, the generic cloud-native schemas act as an empty vessel. Rather than being hardcoded into the compiler core, highly specialized domain intelligence is distributed across the entire extensible Aggrega ecosystem. It is encapsulated within the Platform Catalog through specialized `components`, `features`, and `recipes`. Developers preserve their specific application intent within their `values` and `uses` blocks — strictly governed by the Architect's `schema:` declarations (compact form or full JSON Schema 2020-12) — while the physical translation of that intelligence is executed by target-specific WebAssembly plugins.

925a286772cae701: **Resilience:** `core/fallback-chain` sends a request whose model fails on to other models: `chains` names, for each model alias that falls back, the aliases to try in order until one answers, a fallback that fails following its own entry in turn, and `max_hops` bounds how far along that chain a request is passed. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway by writing both into the routing configuration the gateway's Recipe renders, and halts the build on a name the gateway's model map does not publish. A request falls back only once the gateway has given up on the alias it asked for: where one alias is published more than once, a failed call first moves to another of its entries as a retry, bounded by the gateway's retry count. `core/retry-policy` sets that count — how many times the gateway may send a request, the first send included (`max_attempts`), for a failure that succeeds on being sent again, such as a refused connection, a rate limit or a timeout — and the standard library realizes it on the AI gateway by writing it into the routing configuration the gateway's Recipe renders. On `core/gateway/envoy-gateway` it is realized as the retry of the traffic policy on the route serving the wired models, the same policy that carries a period budget's rate limit, because Envoy Gateway attaches one traffic policy to a route: a request is sent again after a refused connection or stream, a reset or a reply of 429, 503 or 504, up to `max_attempts` sends, and a model that answers nothing within the route's request timeout is not sent again, because that timeout spans every send. On `core/gateway/azure-api-management` it is realized as Azure's retry around the forwarding, in the backend section of the API's policy: a request answered with HTTP 429 or a 5xx status is sent again, its body held so it can be resent, one second after the previous send, up to `max_attempts` sends. A refused or dropped connection, and a model that answers nothing within the forwarding's timeout, are not sent again, because Azure ends the retry on such an error and hands it to the policy's on-error section. Azure retries 1 to 50 times after the first send, so a `max_attempts` of 1 writes no retry and one above 51 is refused by name. The retry takes the place of the forwarding the API would inherit, so while it is attached a forwarding setting made at a broader scope of the instance, such as a timeout, does not apply to the API, which forwards with Azure's defaults. On the hosted gateway, `core/retry-policy` is realized by writing into the gateway's resource its retry count, which names the sends after the first, from 1 to 5, so `max_attempts` from 2 to 6 is honoured and any other value refused; `core/fallback-chain` is not realized there, because that gateway falls back between models only inside a route a request names in place of a model, so a request for a model never falls back. On `core/gateway/kong-enterprise`, `core/fallback-chain` is realized on its chart Recipe: the chat and completion routes of each alias `chains` gives an entry carry Kong's AI Proxy Advanced in place of its AI proxy, with the alias's model and the models its walk falls back to as targets in priority order — the alias, then its entry's fallbacks in order, a fallback's own entry followed in turn only while fewer than `max_hops` have been counted. The balancer sends a request to each target of the walk once, in order, until one answers, moving on after a connection error or timeout, an invalid reply header or a reply of 429, 500, 502, 503 or 504, and returns every other reply as it came. The build halts on a name the `models` socket does not carry, on a walk reaching an alias twice, beside `core/retry-policy`, since Kong keeps one retry count for the whole walk and cannot send to a model again before falling back, and on a gateway image older than 3.12. `core/retry-policy` is not realized there, and its realization halts every attachment naming why: each wired model is served on routes of its own carrying that one model, so a retry has to send the request to that same target again, and Kong's reference reads both ways on whether its balancer does. On `core/gateway/agentgateway`, `core/retry-policy` is realized on the chart Recipe as a retry policy of the gateway's own configuration, attached to the listener its model requests arrive on: a request is sent again, at once and to the same model, after a reply of 429, 500, 502, 503 or 504, a refused or reset connection, a connection taking longer than 11 seconds to open or a failed name lookup, up to `max_attempts` sends. agentgateway sends a request once more than its policy's attempts, so the policy is written as `max_attempts` less one, `max_attempts` 1 writes none, and one above 256 is refused by name. A request whose body is larger than 64 KiB is sent once, and the configuration sets no timeout, so a model that accepts the connection and answers nothing is waited on rather than sent again. `core/fallback-chain` is not realized there, and its realization halts every attachment naming why: agentgateway fails over between models by evicting a failed one for the requests after it, while the request that failed is answered with its failure, so no request is walked along a chain. On `core/gateway/higress`, `core/retry-policy` is realized as the route's own retry, written as Ingress annotations onto every model route: a request is sent again after a refused or reset connection, a 5xx reply or a 429, a POST included, up to `max_attempts` sends; `max_attempts` 1 writes the retry off, overriding the retry Higress's control plane gives a route carrying no annotation, and one above 2147483648 is refused by name. A model that accepts the connection and then answers nothing or slowly is not sent again, since the route sets no per-try deadline, and a streamed request is sent again only before its reply has begun. `core/fallback-chain` is not realized there either, and its realization halts every attachment naming why: Higress sends a failed request on at most once, to one other destination — a route's default backend, or the one fallback route its console writes for an AI route — so no request is walked along a chain. On `core/gateway/traefik-hub` both are realized on the chart Recipe, and each halts the build on a Traefik Hub image older than v3.20, whose failover takes no middlewares on the services it tries and whose retry cannot send a POST again on a reply's status — a retry policy of one send excepted. `core/fallback-chain` sends the route of each alias `chains` gives an entry through nested failovers of Traefik's own, trying the models of the alias's walk in order — the alias, then its entry's fallbacks in order, a fallback's own entry followed in turn only while fewer than `max_hops` have been counted — each with its own model name, credential, quotas and retry. A model's reply of 429 or of 500 to 504, after any retry of that model, moves the request on to the next; any other reply is returned as it came, the last model's whatever it is, and a request body over 1 MiB is refused with HTTP 413 rather than sent. The build halts on a name the `models` socket does not carry and on a walk reaching an alias twice. `core/retry-policy` is Traefik's retry middleware, last on each model route, or on each model a walk tries: a request is sent again at once after a connection that carried nothing to the model and after a reply of 429 or of 500 to 504, a POST included, up to `max_attempts` sends, the first included, and `max_attempts` 1 writes nothing. A reply the gateway forms itself — a refusal of its key check, a guard, the masking or a quota — is never sent again, and neither is a streamed reply once it has begun.
925b5016e2a915cd: **One shape on that open surface halts: a fill written on the component under another name.** When an attachment written on the component itself — on its own `features:` block in the Aggregate, or on the Release's entry for that one component — carries a name no slot declares, and its Feature satisfies the `selector` of a slot that nothing binds on that component once every scope has folded, the build halts. That is the shape a fill meant for the slot takes when it is written under the wrong name: left alone it would be a free attachment while the slot stays empty, and an optional slot left empty builds green and delivers nothing. The message names the attachment, the component, the Feature and each empty slot that Feature fits, and the remedy is to attach it under the slot's name. It holds for every Feature, not only for credentials. Everything else on the surface stays free: an attachment whose Feature fits no declared slot, an extra attachment once every slot it fits is bound, and an attachment the component inherits from a subsystem or a Release boundary — so the shared shape above is untouched. A slot declaring no `selector` says nothing about which Feature it is for, so no attachment is held to it this way. The halt is described in [errors/fatal-halts.md](../errors/fatal-halts.md) under "An attachment written under another name fits a slot its component leaves empty".

9af7fc0e9e1b4854: **The Aggrega Solution:** This check runs ahead of time. Because Aggrega builds a complete IR graph of the intended topology in memory, a governance verdict role can run advanced pathfinding rules across the entire architecture. If the policy detects a continuous, transitive chain of edges originating from a public node and terminating at a highly sensitive database with none of the controls the enterprise requires attached anywhere along it, it immediately halts the build. The insecure architecture is blocked before a single line of infrastructure code is ever generated.
9b10e8d240ad1a6b: **What the standard library carries today.** `core/ai-tool/mcp` carries `http`. It attaches a Model Context Protocol server to an agent, and the Manifest chooses how that server is realized: `helm/mcp` runs an image serving the protocol over HTTP; `helm/mcp-stdio-bridge` and `compose/mcp-stdio-bridge` run a package that speaks only stdio behind a pinned bridge serving it over HTTP; `helm/mcp-remote` and `compose/mcp-remote` reach a server someone else runs, and run nothing. Every realization publishes the same `host`, `port`, `endpoint`, `protocol` and `credential_header`, so a consumer's wiring does not change with the realization. A bridged server's credentials are environment variables, held in the tool's `server_env` slot and delivered to the bridge by reference on Kubernetes; a remote server's credential is held by the consumer on its own connection to the tool and presented under the header `credential_header` names, `Authorization` unless the Release names another. Where a remote server reads its key from its own address, the consumer holds the whole address on that connection too, in an `endpoint` slot filled on Kubernetes by a reference to a Secret and on Docker Compose by a Compose variable reference, so the key reaches no rendered file, while the tool's `infra.endpoint` holds the address without the part that carries the key; [examples/mcp-address-from-secret](../language-reference/examples/mcp-address-from-secret/) builds both. `core/ai-agent/openai-agents-sdk`, `core/ai-agent/claude-agent-sdk`, `core/ai-agent/agent-framework`, `core/ai-agent/google-adk` and `core/ai-agent/mastra`, and the flow platforms `core/ai-agent/flowise` and `core/ai-agent/n8n`, declare a tool socket of this form, `tools`, and deliver each wired tool's address, and the connection's credential by reference, under variables named for the connection's alias; a consumer of its own declares one the same way. 9b22ccabe1e2c696:
**Action:** The CLI fetches all requested entities (Components, Features, Releases). It first checks these definitions for the `extends` keyword. For the Catalog entities, it deep-merges the YAML metadata, and the two kinds part company on the data pillars: a Feature's `schema:` composes with its base's under JSON Schema 2020-12 composition, while an extending Component composes structure only — its attachment slots, topology sockets, self-inject allowlist and named assertions — and receives its base's `schema:` block exactly as the base authored it. An extending `Release` folds by the same rule: the child's value wins key by key, down to the first indivisible value — a scalar, a list, a template — which replaces whole, and a key the child writes as `null` is removed. So its whole authoring surface travels — the boundary tree with its per-component `infra` and Feature attachments, the `parameters` block, the annotations, and the Manifest pointer — while no `metadata` field does, since identity and provenance are per-Release.
Next, it performs an in-memory interpolation in three sub-steps: parameter contract validation against the Aggregate's typed `parameters:` declarations; interpolation of the resolved values into the surrounding `values:` strings; withdrawal of the `.parameters` map from every value-template context, leaving it readable to operator-authored path templates alone. Finally, it injects the resolved `infra` blocks into the target component payloads. Once the blueprint is fully concrete, the compiler uses the unified `schema:` declaration from the Catalog (compact form or full JSON Schema 2020-12) to strictly validate the developer's `values` and `infra` configurations locally.

a6e4de34151fb189: **Period budget:** `core/period-budget` bounds what the traffic through a gateway may consume over a period: a `limit`, the `period` it covers, a `scope` — everything the gateway serves, each caller or each model — and a `unit` — a cost in US dollars or tokens — and once what the gateway has counted over the period exceeds the limit, further model requests are refused. It attaches to any component declaring `dataplane.aggrega.ai/period-budget`. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway, whose budget covers everything the gateway serves, is counted in US dollars, and starts again at the start of every period — a number of days from midnight UTC, or a calendar month from its first day: the realization writes the limit and the period into the configuration the gateway's Recipe renders, refuses any other unit, scope or period by name — `30d` among them, which the gateway counts as a calendar month — and halts unless the gateway's `database_url` and `api_key` credential slots are both attached, because without its bookkeeping database the gateway keeps no count and without an administrative key it checks no caller against the budget. Once the count exceeds the limit, the gateway refuses the administrative key's model requests as well as every caller's; its model listing and key management still answer that key. On the hosted gateway it is realized as a spend-limit rule on the gateway's resource, counted in US dollars over a window that moves forward with time — the last `period`, for models whose pricing the gateway knows — for everything the gateway serves: a budget per caller or per model, tokens and a calendar month are refused by name. On `core/gateway/apisix` it is realized on the chart Recipe, written onto the routes of the wired models as APISIX's token rate limiting: counted in the tokens each model's reply reports — `total_tokens`, `prompt_tokens` or `completion_tokens` — over a fixed window of `period` that opens with the first model request after the previous window closed rather than on the clock, for everything the gateway serves, for each wired model apart, or for each caller its Release declares in `infra.callers` apart, the gateway telling them apart by the key each presents. Once the count reaches the limit the gateway answers model requests with HTTP 503 until the window closes; a request's tokens are added once its reply completes, so the request that reaches the limit is served, and a reply its semantic cache serves counts nothing and is served past the limit. APISIX counts no tokens on a completion request, so while the budget is attached each wired model gets its chat route alone, and it keeps the count in the memory of the gateway process, so the chart runs one replica and a restart opens a new window. A budget in US dollars, one per caller while `infra.callers` declares none, a calendar month and a second budget on one gateway are refused by name, as is an attachment on its workload Recipe, which renders no route. On `core/gateway/envoy-gateway` it is realized as Envoy Gateway's usage-based rate limit, on the AI route serving the models wired to the gateway: the route declares the token count `unit` names — `total_tokens`, `prompt_tokens` or `completion_tokens` — as a cost Envoy AI Gateway reads off each reply, and a traffic policy on that route charges it when the reply completes, against `limit` tokens per one unit of Envoy Gateway's rate limit, for everything the gateway serves or for each wired model apart. Each window is fixed on the UTC clock — a second, a minute, an hour, a day from midnight, a week from a Thursday, or 30 or 365 days counted from 1 January 1970 — and `1mo` is a calendar month, under a setting of Envoy Gateway's rate-limit service that then holds for every monthly rate limit that install keeps. The count is kept by the rate-limit service Envoy Gateway's control plane creates and turns on for every gateway it serves, in the Redis-protocol store wired to the gateway's `cache` socket. Once the count exceeds the limit the gateway answers model requests with HTTP 429 until the window ends; a request's tokens are added once its reply completes, so the request that crosses the limit is served. While the store or the rate-limit service cannot be reached, or a check takes longer than Envoy's rate-limit timeout, model requests are refused with HTTP 500, under a setting of Envoy Gateway's control plane that then holds for every rate limit that install keeps, so a rate limit applied to it by hand fails closed too; a request admitted just before an outage is still served and not counted, because its tokens are charged after the reply, and a store keeping the count in memory starts every window again when it restarts. A budget in US dollars, one per caller — the gateway tells callers apart only by a header the caller writes itself, and nothing on that path verifies it — any other period and a second budget on one gateway are refused by name, as is an attachment with nothing wired to the `models` or the `cache` socket. On `core/gateway/azure-api-management` it is realized as Azure's token limit, written into the API's policy: counted in the prompt and completion tokens each reply reports, together, for everything the API serves or for each API Management subscription, whose key the gateway verifies — either a quota over a fixed window on the UTC clock, an hour, a day, a week, a calendar month or a calendar year (`1h`, `1d`, `7d`, `1mo` or `12mo`; Microsoft does not say which day a week starts on), answered with HTTP 403 once exceeded, or a rate over one minute (`1m`), answered with HTTP 429 and counted over a sliding window on the classic tiers and as a token bucket on the v2 tiers. The count is the usage each reply reports, so concurrent requests can pass the limit, and each gateway of the instance keeps its own count. A budget in US dollars or in prompt or completion tokens alone, one per model — the model a request names is written by the caller, and several names can reach one model — one per subscription on an API that requires no subscription key, any other period and a limit that is not a whole number are refused by name. The Consumption tier runs no token limit. On `core/gateway/kong-enterprise` it is realized on the chart Recipe, written into the routes the gateway imports as Kong's AI Rate Limiting Advanced: counted in the tokens each model's reply reports — `total_tokens`, `prompt_tokens` or `completion_tokens` — in fixed windows of `period`, a number of seconds, minutes, hours or days, each request counted in the one window its time falls in, for everything the gateway serves or for each wired model apart, a request under scope `model` counted against the alias it named whichever model answered it. Once the count reaches the limit the next model request is answered with HTTP 429 until the window ends, so the request that crosses the limit is served; Kong can also refuse a request early, on its own estimate of the prompt tokens it carries. The count is kept in the gateway's PostgreSQL backend, shared by every replica and kept across a restart. A budget in US dollars — Kong counts cost only from a price its configuration gives each model, and the catalog supplies none — one per caller — Kong tells callers apart only as the consumers an authentication plugin names, and the gateway declares no callers, for the reasons "Kong in front of models" above gives — a calendar month, a second budget on one gateway and a gateway image older than 3.15 are refused by name, as is an attachment with nothing wired to the `models` socket. On `core/gateway/agentgateway` it is realized on the chart Recipe, written into the gateway's configuration and counted in the total tokens each reply reports: under scope `caller` as a budget on the API key of each caller its Release declares in `infra.callers`, over fixed windows of `period` aligned to the Unix epoch, a day starting at midnight UTC, kept in a SQLite store on a volume the Recipe renders, with one replica; under scope `gateway` or `model` as a token bucket for everything the gateway serves or for each model name a request asks for, filled to the limit every `period` from when the gateway read its configuration and kept in its memory, so a restart or a changed configuration fills it again. Once what was counted reaches the limit, model requests are answered with HTTP 429 until the window ends or the bucket is filled; the request that reaches it is served. A budget in US dollars — the gateway's model cost catalog prices none of the models wired to it, so the budget would count nothing — in prompt or completion tokens alone, one per caller while `infra.callers` declares none, a calendar month, a limit that is not a whole number and a second budget on one gateway are refused by name, as is an attachment with nothing wired to the `models` socket; its compose Recipe has no realization of it. On `core/gateway/traefik-hub` it is realized on the chart Recipe as Traefik Hub's quota middleware on the route of each wired model, keeping its count in the Redis-protocol store wired to the gateway's `cache` socket: it counts the tokens each reply reports — `total_tokens`, `prompt_tokens` or `completion_tokens` — or, under `usd`, their cost in US dollars, priced from a list of models the middleware ships with, a model it has no price for being refused with HTTP 422, over a window that slides with time, what was counted at one moment freeing again one period later, for each wired model apart, or for everything the gateway serves while one model is wired. Once the count reaches the limit, model requests are refused with HTTP 429; a request's count is added once its reply completes, so the request crossing the limit, and any served beside it, is served, and a reply the semantic cache serves counts nothing. Traefik's reference says the quota serves requests uncounted while the store cannot be reached. A budget per caller — the quota tells requests apart by the client's address, a request header or the request's host, and none of them is the caller the gateway's key check verified — one for the whole gateway while several models are wired, since Traefik's reference does not say whether routes naming one quota share its count, a calendar month and any period but hours or days, or minutes or seconds making whole hours, are refused by name, as are a limit that is not a whole number of tokens and an attachment with nothing wired to the `models` or the `cache` socket. On `core/gateway/higress` it is realized on the chart Recipe as Higress's token limit plugin on the route of each wired model, keeping its count in the Redis-protocol store wired to the gateway's `cache` socket: it adds the prompt and completion tokens each reply reports, together, once the reply completes, over a fixed window of `period` — a second, a minute, an hour or a day — that opens when the first reply in it is counted, for everything the gateway serves or for each alias apart. While the count exceeds the limit, model requests are answered with HTTP 429 until the window ends, so the request crossing the limit is served. A reply reporting no usage counts nothing, so the Recipe asks a streamed request's model to report its usage and refuses with HTTP 403 a streamed request turning that report off, a request whose content type neither contains `application/json` nor begins with `multipart/form-data`, which the AI proxy forwards without asking for the report, and one whose body the gateway's plugins do not read — a compressed body, a content type containing `octet-stream` or `grpc`, an upgrade; a client deliberately sending a body the gateway's validation cannot decode gets past those refusals, and such a streamed request goes uncounted. With no masking attached, a request whose body exceeds the gateway's 32 KiB buffer may be refused with HTTP 413, depending on when the store answers. While the store cannot be reached, model requests are served and not counted: the plugin has no setting that refuses them then. A budget in US dollars or in prompt or completion tokens alone, one per caller — the gateway declares no callers, so it verifies none — any other period, a limit that is not a whole number and a second budget on one gateway are refused by name, as is an attachment with nothing wired to the `models` or the `cache` socket.

The AI gateway, the two Kongs, APISIX and agentgateway deliver each wired model's key under a variable of its own, which that model's entry or route in their configuration names; Envoy Gateway names the Secret in the security policy of the model's backend, and Envoy AI Gateway's controller reads the key from it; Traefik Hub names the Secret and the data key in the Chat Completion middleware of the model's route, and reads the key from it. A connection reaching a model labelled `component.aggrega.ai/hosting: managed` carries one, or says in its own `values` that the model takes none, `unauthenticated: true`; with neither, the caller's assertion halts the build naming the connection and its target, and a model labelled otherwise draws no such halt. Neither end sees the other's attachments, so the server learns nothing of a caller's key, and the two match because the Aggregate feeds both from one parameter: where both ends resolve secrets in one scope — one Kubernetes namespace, one Compose project — they reference one secret, and otherwise each holds its own, realized from the same store entry. vLLM, TEI and TGI each check a single key, so every caller presents the same key and the server cannot tell its callers apart, and TGI matches its key without regard to letter case; APISIX, agentgateway and Traefik Hub each check every declared caller's key and tell their callers apart by it; the two Kongs declare no callers and check no caller's key, for the reasons "Kong in front of models" above gives; the LiteLLM model and the AI gateway also accept the keys they issue, while their bookkeeping database is attached. **Domain 2: The Split Schema (`usesSchema` & `schema`)**
To prevent the Platform Catalog from fragmenting into unmanageable schema files, Aggrega utilizes a Split Schema engine. The Native YAML `usesSchema` strictly defines and validates the topology, while `schema:` (JSON Schema 2020-12 — typically authored via the compact-form shorthand) validates the content of the `values` and `infra` pillars and declares the shape of the `provides` pillar. The `values` a developer authors and the `infra` an operator sets are checked against their declared types; the `provides` sub-schema declares the key names and types of the downstream contract a Recipe produces, and the compiler checks that every `inject` reference names a declared `provides` key — but the produced `provides` values themselves travel downstream as opaque strings the compiler pipes without interpretation, not values it type-checks, because the core does not interpret what a piped value means. **The `usesSchema` is where a socket is *declared*, and declaring one is what gives it a contract.** A socket the catalog entity declares carries that entity's constraints: a selector saying which targets it may reach, an `inject` allowlist, and per-edge `valueSchema` / `infraSchema`. Inside the `usesSchema`, Platform Architects use the `selector:` field — read as the string the Architect wrote, not copied into any generated schema — and the native Go selector engine evaluates it to enforce **Cross-Node Type Safety** over declared sockets. It ensures that if a socket requires a database, the developer cannot plug in a web server.

At inject hydration, which runs next, the compiler walks `uses:` edges and resolves each caller's `.context.uses.<alias>.provides.<provided-name>` against the resolved provides values. performs declares how far its own effects travel — `none` for one that reads or renders and leaves
nothing behind, `workspace` for one that writes inside the workspace this process serves, `registry`
for one that publishes, signs or withdraws, and `machine` for one that changes what every workspace on
the host shares. Naming a kind here withdraws every tool that reaches it: the tool is absent from
every caller's tool list whatever that caller's token carries, and a call to it is refused naming this
setting. That makes it the deployment's bound rather than the caller's, and no credential lifts it — a
server meant to serve reads and nothing else lists the three writing kinds here and then cannot
publish even for a caller whose token carries every scope. Leave it out, which is the default, and
this deployment carries whatever its callers' scopes admit. A value that is not one of the four is
refused when this file loads, rather than passed over. Nothing of the `machine` kind is offered over
HTTP whatever this says, so naming it is accepted and changes nothing;
[aggrega-mcp.md](aggrega-mcp.md#what-a-caller-may-reach) sets out the kinds and the scopes that admit
them.

**`mcp.authorization.issuer` and `mcp.authorization.resource` say who issues the tokens callers
present, and what this server is called as the resource they are issued for.** Both are required
whenever the `http` transport is chosen, and a listener is refused before anything binds without them, because
every request to the endpoint is answered with a bearer-token challenge and a challenge that names
nowhere to go is one a client cannot act on. Write whole addresses, scheme and host included: the
issuer exactly as that authorization server states its own identifier, and the resource as the
address your callers actually reach — the host a proxy in front presents, where there is one, rather
than the address this process binds. Both are published, with no credential asked for, in the OAuth
protected-resource metadata document the listener serves, which is where a client looks to find out
where to obtain a token. Neither holds anything secret: a token arrives on the request that
presents it and is never written in a configuration file. The issuer is an `https` address unless
the authorization server runs on this machine — `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `::1` — and a listener
naming a plain `http` issuer on any other host is refused before anything binds, whichever way it
reads its keys and its callers: every client is sent to the issuer to obtain its token, so over plain
`http` its authorization code and its token would cross the network unprotected, and where the keys
are read from there too, whoever sits on that path could substitute them.

of reading them from the authorization server. Leave it out and the server reads that server's

is found wherever the server is launched from. The file holds public verification keys, which are
what an authorization server publishes — nothing that signs, and nothing secret.

At the **gateway hop**, the developer attaches `core/context-propagation` to the gateway a request enters through, which selects on `dataplane.aggrega.ai/caller-identity`. At **compile-time**, the attachment is realized in that gateway's own configuration — on Envoy Gateway, a client traffic policy that verifies each client's certificate against an authority the Release names and forwards the certificate's details; on the LiteLLM AI gateway, a request hook that removes any identity header a caller supplied and adds the user and team of the virtual key the gateway verified, and its organization where the key names one, on requests to the model aliases the attachment lists in `destinations`. At the **workload hop**, a request one agent makes directly to another never crosses that gateway, so it is checked at the receiving agent's own ingress, where a service mesh rejects any request lacking a signed token proving the original user's intent (e.g., an Istio JWT `AuthorizationPolicy`). The standard library ships the gateway-hop Feature and no workload-hop Feature, so attaching `core/context-propagation` protects the traffic that passes through a gateway and leaves agent-to-agent calls to mesh configuration the enterprise supplies itself. An agent another party runs, which `core/ai-tool/agent-invocation` reaches over A2A as `core/ai-agent/a2a-remote`, sits outside the Release altogether: that party checks each call against the security scheme the agent's Agent Card declares, and the tool presents the credential held on its connection, read from a Secret by reference, under the request header the agent publishes. Where the card requires OAuth 2.0 client credentials or OpenID Connect, the connection holds a client secret instead, or as well, with the client id the operator writes on it, and the agent publishes the token or discovery address and the scopes its card declares; the tool's own container obtains the token with them, refreshes it and presents it on each call; the catalog delivers only those inputs, and no build can check what the container does with them. Where the card requires mutual TLS, the connection holds a client certificate, and, where an authority the image does not already trust signs the agent's server certificate, that authority too; each is mounted into the tool's container as files from a Secret the connection names, and the container presents the certificate in the TLS handshake itself. It does not reach one whose card requires a key in the query string, an HTTP scheme answering a challenge from the agent, such as Digest, or an OAuth 2.0 flow other than client credentials. Nor does it present a credential to an agent another party runs over plain HTTP: where that agent's address is `http`, a credential or a client secret on the connection halts the build, naming the connection, because the credential, or the token obtained with the secret, would travel to it unencrypted. **Directories listed under `workspace.catalog_dirs` are read as well, and they are read first.**
The list is an ordered search stack: the first directory to declare an identity owns it, and the
same identity in a later directory is shadowed. `catalog` is read after everything listed — unless
a listed directory already contains it, in which case it is read as part of that directory — so
listing a directory adds to what you had rather than replacing it. A repeatable `--catalog <dir>`
on the command line is read ahead of both, and a relative path given there resolves against the
directory you ran the command from, since no configuration file declared it. A directory named more
than once — on the command line and in the list, or twice in the list — is read once, at the place it
was first named, so nothing in it is reported as shadowed by itself: a shadow is always two different
files declaring one identity. Two spellings of one directory, a path to it through a link, and — on a
file system that ignores case — a spelling in another case all name that one directory. A directory
inside another listed directory is still read as its own entry. A project that keeps a
catalog variant per Release can give each Release a list of its own instead — see
[Giving a Release its own catalog directories](#giving-a-release-its-own-catalog-directories).

dbc0f2ee86410882: **Concurrency:** `core/concurrency-limit` caps how many requests a gateway carries at once (`max_in_flight`), which keeps a burst of callers from becoming a queue at the model behind it. `scope` says what one cap counts: `gateway`, the default, counts every request the gateway forwards together; `model` gives each target the gateway sends requests to a count of its own, a target being each upstream entry the gateway routes to, so where one model name has several entries each is counted apart. The cap and its scope are capacity sizing the operator decides, set in the attachment's `infra`, so the operator attaches it in the Release. The cap is counted per running proxy, so where several replicas run each of them admits that many. It attaches to any component declaring `dataplane.aggrega.ai/concurrency-cap`, and a realization refuses by name the scope its gateway does not count. On `core/gateway/nginx` scope `gateway` is realized as NGINX's `limit_conn`, keyed on one word the same for every request, so NGINX counts every request it is processing as one total, kept in memory its worker processes share, and answers a request past the cap with HTTP 503; scope `model` is refused, since NGINX keeps no count for each upstream target, and so is a `max_in_flight` above 65535, the most `limit_conn` takes. On `core/gateway/envoy-gateway` scope `model` is realized as the circuit breaker of the traffic policy on the route serving the wired models, the policy that also carries a period budget's rate limit and the retry policy's retry: Envoy Gateway applies it to the backend of each rule of that route, and each wired model has a rule of its own, so at most `max_in_flight` requests are sent to each wired model at once, and a request past the cap is answered with HTTP 503 and is not sent again; a send the retry policy repeats counts against the cap like the first. Envoy's worker threads check the count and then add to it, so requests arriving together can take it briefly above the cap. Scope `gateway` is refused, since Envoy Gateway keeps a cap for each backend and none on their total, and so is an attachment with nothing wired to the `models` socket. On the AI gateway scope `model` is realized as the `max_parallel_requests` of every entry of its model map, typed by hand and wired alike: at most `max_in_flight` requests are in flight to each entry at once, and a request finding its entry full is answered with HTTP 429 — after the gateway's retries where its alias has one entry, and at once where it has several, even while another of them has room, since the proxy picks the entry before it counts — unless `core/fallback-chain` lists fallbacks for its alias, to which it is then sent on. The proxy keeps each count in memory, where by default a record lapses ten minutes after it is made and a new count then starts at zero, so the attachment also sets that lifetime to a century, keeping every count as long as the proxy runs. Because of that lifetime the gateway refuses a request carrying `priority` while the cap is attached, even where the Release admits the field, since the proxy keeps a queue entry for every such request until its record lapses; and the build halts on a model map of more than 100 entries, past which the store the counts are kept in, which holds 200 records and drops one whenever it is full, could drop a count. Scope `gateway` is refused there, since the proxy's one total is read only by a request limiter an environment variable switches on, which counts a request for its first second. Nor does the hosted gateway realize it: the request limit its terraform Recipe writes into the gateway's resource is a rate, a number of requests over an interval, rather than a cap on the requests in flight.

ddccb91a96b234ad: The architect authors **Components** and **Features**: the reusable, versioned contracts developers consume. **(D) The Dynamic Business Context (Cascading Annotations)**
While `labels` define the immutable Catalog DNA, dynamic business contexts (like SOC2 audit scoping or FinOps cost tracking) change depending on who deploys the application and where it runs. **`mcp.announce_tools` narrows what the server announces, and it is a different bound from the key
above.** Name the tools this server announces, spelled as the tool list reports them, and exactly
those are announced: one left out is absent from every caller's tool list and refused if it is called

carries is announced; write an empty list and none is, so those two spellings are different
statements and no default is filled in for you. What separates it from `deny_reach` is what each one
takes away. `deny_reach` takes away a capability: the operations of a withdrawn kind are not carried
here at all and no credential brings one back. `announce_tools` takes away only an announcement — the
tools it leaves out are capabilities the server still has — and what it answers is a client that caps
how many tools it will register, sometimes across every server it is connected to at once. Where both
are set the withdrawal wins, so a tool of a withdrawn kind stays absent however this key names it. A
name no tool answers to stops the server before it serves anything, listing the tools it does have,
rather than leaving you with a surface narrower than the one you asked for. Unlike the other keys
here, which configure the listener the `http` transport starts, it is read whichever transport the server
speaks, because the client a narrowing exists for is usually the one that launched the process over

The step records that plugin — its reference and the digest of its entity — and the exact rules it composed in the `entity.lock`. From then on, every reading of the directory applies the recorded rules and no others: a publication of the entity, the comparison a pull or a push holds the lock to, the entity's row in a lockfile, a build's comparison, the render that hands the directory to a provider, and `aggrega pull --verify`. fc8b4f8bd533abdb: **The document comes from the kind's own contract and from nothing else.** It is not a worked example. There is no namespace, no category, no label values filled in for you, and no commented suggestion of what people usually write — because none of those is something the compiler requires. A catalog chooses its own naming, its own categories and its own directory layout; the schema decides the fields, and the schema is all this command reads. A starter document that guessed at the rest would teach you a rule that does not exist.
fc981e4417146b73: Platform Architects use the `extends` keyword to layer specialized interfaces on top of corporate or community baselines. Extending **composes structure** and **inherits the data pillars whole**. The compiler walks the chain from the base down; the two halves behave differently, and the difference is the whole authoring model.

fca1f2c6823ec5ed: **A push refuses an entity whose lock does not record those pins.** Before it builds the bundle, a push works out what the pin step would record for the entity and compares it with the `entity.lock` beside it. Where a pin is missing, or the lock holds one an input no longer matches, the push stops before any archive is built or any registry is contacted. The refusal names the entity and every such input — each a `remote source`, an `imported file` or a `local source file` — and what to run: `aggrega pin` on the entity, `--pin-sources` on the push you just ran, or `pin_sources_at_push` for every push in the workspace. It is the same refusal a pull raises over the same lock, [An entity reads an input the lock beside it records no pin for](../errors/fatal-halts.md#an-entity-reads-an-input-the-lock-beside-it-records-no-pin-for), with a push's own remedies. So a Recipe or FeatureRecipe a push publishes carries, inside its bundle, a lock recording every pin the step would have recorded at the moment it was published.

A request for an unpinned URL halts, naming the URL and the step that pins it; there is no setting that turns that halt into a fetch, because quietly widening the set of inputs a build reads is the one thing a reproducible build must not do.

**The command line reports that same walk as a non-zero exit, and which reader you are decides what
that exit is worth.** For a person at a terminal it is not the whole account: `aggrega registry update`
prints how many of the selected registries it indexed, what each one found, which ones it did not
index, and where the index was written — so the summary says what happened and the exit status says
only whether all of it succeeded. For a script it is the whole account, because that command offers no
structured output mode, so its exit status is the only machine-readable verdict available. That is why
the two surfaces answer the same partial walk differently and both are right: this one hands a
structured caller `failed` and succeeds, while the command line has one bit to spend and spends it on
"was any registry missed".

**Nothing is prompted for.** Nobody is watching this stream, so identity is resolved from a supplied
or ambient credential source and never by asking. Where the terminal command would have put a question
to a person — a registry that needs credentials, a capability more than one provider plugin serves,
the text a withdrawal is to carry — the request fails with a message naming what to supply rather than
blocking on an answer that will never arrive. A refusal leaves the workspace exactly as it was: no
lockfile is written and no partial record is left behind, and a publication that could not resolve a
credential refuses before any bytes reach the registry.
